verdict.reasoning: Patient reports new swelling of the elbow for about a week and that it is the left elbow: “I just noticed this like about a week ago… have like a weird swelling on… my elbow” and later, “it's the, the left elbow.”

Warmth and fluid sensation: “it's, it's slightly warm… I cannot feel like this, little bit fluid in inside”; tenderness pattern: “On the tip of the elbow, it's, it's OK, just like, next to it like where the, the swelling is, it's a bit, yeah it feels weird.”
Patient reports preserved movement: “I can actually like move it normally.” This supports full range of motion in the elbow.

No trauma: “have you banged that elbow?… Patient: No, not really… I haven't noticed anything”; first episode: “No, no I haven't noticed that before. Um, I don't have any like history of, of seeing this.”
Desk job: “No, I just, you know sit at a desk”; running 2–3 times/week: “I run regularly, like two, three times a week.”

Osteoarthritis diagnosed by GP: patient says, “I think I have something like uh, osteoarthritis,” and when asked, “Has anyone ever told you that?” replies, “Um, yes. Yes, a few years ago.” When asked who: “a a GP.”
Food allergy: “I'm, I'm allergic to, to peanuts”; drug allergies denied: “are you allergic to any medication? Patient: Uh, no. Not that I know of.”
No regular medications: “do you um, are you on any medication on a regular basis? Patient: Uh, no.”

The exam via video is described only partially: visible swelling and warmth and dry skin are mentioned (“I noticed the skin was a bit dry…,” “It's a bit warmer”), but there is no explicit statement of “olecranon” location, no measured ‘mild’ tenderness, and no restatement of full active range of motion in the exam portion; these details are added beyond the transcript.

Diagnosis and atraumatic nature: “this seems like uh, what we call the Bursitis” in the context of the elbow, and earlier confirmed as left elbow; no trauma: “have you banged that elbow?… Patient: No, not really.” This supports atraumatic left olecranon bursitis.

Specific ibuprofen plan: “I would take Ibuprofen regularly… that's four hundred milligrams, two times a day. And you should take, take that after food, not on an empty stomach. If you get any heartburn, stop taking it.” Dyspepsia/heartburn stopping advice is explicitly given.

Blood tests and mailing forms: “what I would like to do, is to get some blood tests done… check for inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies… and also check for things like Gout as well,” and “arrange some, um, blood test forms to be sent out to your house.” FBC, ESR/CRP, uric acid, and rheumatoid antibodies are standard names for what is described.

Follow-up modality and timing: “we can arrange a follow-up appointment… doesn't have to be face-to-face… we can do that over the phone, uh, over video,” and results expected in “about five or six days… we're looking maybe six days.” This supports follow-up around one week after labs via video or in person.

Urgent care warning: “if your… elbow was to become very red, very painful, uh, and the redness was to spread or become uh, you know more intense. Then you need to get on the phone or get, have a video appointment… as soon as possible. 'Cause that would be an emergency.”
